title: Goldman Sachs Limits AI Coding Tools To Engineers Only
excerpt: Internal guidance updated in October ends months of Claude Code and GitHub access for most bankers and traders, months after the bank's tech chief praised their 'vibe coding.'
body:
• Goldman Sachs has limited Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its engineers, ending months of access for most bankers and traders, Bloomberg reported.
  • The change came in internal guidance updated in October, after the bank assessed factors including productivity and risk management.
  • Strats — staff who combine trading, quantitative research and software engineering — keep access, according to a person familiar with the matter.
  • For finance professionals: tools you prototyped with may now need an engineer sponsor — route AI-built tools through engineering rather than running them on the desk.

Goldman Sachs has restricted advanced AI coding tools to its engineers, cutting off most bankers and traders after a review of productivity and risk, Bloomberg News reported on Monday. Internal guidance updated in October limits Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to the bank's engineers, PYMNTS reported. Strats, who work across trading, quantitative research and software engineering, still have access, according to a second person familiar with the matter cited by The State of AI.

What traders were doing with the tools

For months, bankers and traders had used the tools on the job. A person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that some traders used them to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and put together written and graphic material — and that the change has frustrated some traders. Those uses went well beyond writing software: coding agents that can read files, write programs and run them had become general-purpose desk assistants for staff who do not code for a living.

https://x.com/BoringBiz_/status/2117324473946743085
"We make certain AI tools available to our people to determine the best use cases across different parts of the firm. After a period of experimentation where we assess a variety of factors including productivity and risk management, we put them in the hands of those who are best suited to leverage them for the long term."

That statement, from Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra, frames the move as the end of an experimentation phase rather than a ban driven by a single incident. No incident behind the decision has been reported. The bank's in-house AI assistant, which draws on models from OpenAI, Alphabet and Anthropic, remains available, and the restriction targets third-party agents that can write and run code themselves.

A reversal from July's "vibe coding" praise

As recently as July, Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti was praising "vibe coding" by non-technical employees. Traders and bankers built solutions with AI tools and passed them to one of the firm's 12,000 engineers to refine, he said. That model let the people closest to a problem build a first version without waiting for engineering time. It also meant staff without engineering training were running code-writing software on machines used to handle client information. Techstrong.ai noted that AI coding agents operate under the permissions of their users, which on a trading desk raises governance questions around material non-public information, data barriers and auditing code that was never vetted. Goldman had already applied narrower limits earlier this year, restricting Claude use for staff in Hong Kong in April, according to The State of AI.

Wall Street is drawing similar lines

Goldman is not alone in tightening controls this fall. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned of "rogue agents" during a third-quarter earnings call last month and said outside AI agents would not be permitted inside the bank, PYMNTS reported. The Goldman decision also lands at an awkward moment: Goldman and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters on Anthropic's planned initial public offering, according to the S-1 filed October 26, The State of AI reported — so over the next few weeks, Goldman's bankers will be marketing shares in a company whose coding agent most of them can no longer use. For traders and bankers who built daily workflows around the tools, Bloomberg's reporting points to no immediate internal replacement, leaving engineering teams as the route for work the desk used to do itself.
